title: Proposals in Timms review for changes to Pip would lead to higher welfare bill, IFS says – UK politics live
description:
Social security minister has been overseeing review designed to ‘rehumanise’ the system but Tories say it will lead to higher spending and fewer checks

  • Ministers approve fast-track disability payments in England and Wales

Q: [From Ali Fortescue from Sky News] We have done an interview with Rishi Sunak who says he is very concerned about the rise of ethnonationalism, and particularly with the suggestion from Suella Braverman, Reform UK’s education spokesperson, that people of Asian heritage can’t be English. Do you agree with him about that, and are you going to do anything about it?
text: Timms gives statement to MPs on his Pip review, setting out its three key conclusions
In the Commons, Stephen Timms is now delivering his statement on Pip.
He says Pip provides “vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long term health conditions”. It was introduced 13 years ago, but has not been reviewed since then.

He says it was co-produced by himself, his two co-chair and 12 other members of a steering group. Almost all of those 12 people had “lived experience of disability or long term ill health”. Every member – including Timms himself – had just one vote, he says.

double quotation mark The review is clear that Pip remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First of all, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It doesn’t consider people’s needs, their aspirations, their barriers, or their extra costs. It’s just about what somebody cannot do. Many people find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and it too often leaves people fearing that work, health, treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it. Second, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution toward the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey reviewed by the steering group showed that Pip does not always target the highest levels of support on those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions reflecting individual circumstances better. And third, the system’s offers offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support that they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.
Badenoch critcises Farage for jibe about her husband voting remain, saying families should be off limits

Kemi Badenoch has criticised Nigel Farage for making a jibe about her remain-voting husband at his press conference this morning. (See 10.51am.) As Sky News reports, asked about Farage’s comment, she told broadcasters:

double quotation markPoliticians go into politics, and our families should not be fair game. Someone has recently been sentenced to prison because of death threats sent not just to me, but actually to my husband directly. We need to keep people’s families out of this. And I think that it is a shame that Nigel Farage is feeling so irrelevant and desperate that he is now talking about attacking my husband for voting remain.
Disability charities welcome Timms review recommendations
Disability and health charities have broadly welcomed the Timms review. Here are some of their comments.
From Jon Sparkes, chief executive of Mencap, the learning disability charity

double quotation markPeople with a learning disability face significant unavoidable extra costs every day. Many tell us that applying for support through Pip is difficult, while repeated reassessments can feel unnecessary and stressful. Changes to make it kinder and more humane are desperately needed. We are very pleased that the Timms review has listened to the thousands of people who have campaigned with us for an end to unnecessary reassessments for people with lifelong conditions.
From David Newbold, director of community at Parkinson’s UK

double quotation markFor well over a decade, people with Parkinson’s have been more likely to be inaccurately assessed for Pip than those with other conditions. This is unfair and should not have been allowed to go on for so long. That’s why we’re delighted to see the Timms review recommend changes we’ve been campaigning for. We’ve long called for better training for Pip assessors, assessments that properly recognise fluctuating symptoms and an end to unnecessary reviews for people with lifelong, progressive conditions. It’s fantastic to see these calls reflected in the recommendations. We’re also pleased to see the commitment to keeping Pip as a cash benefit, although we await further details of what this will mean in practice.
From James Taylor, executive director of strategy at Scope, the disability equality charity

double quotation markThe government’s commitments to fast-tracking claims for people with severe, well-evidenced conditions and cutting unnecessary reviews are positive steps. Disabled people with lifelong conditions shouldn’t have to keep proving they need Pip … The review’s recommendation to keep cash at the heart of Pip is the right one. Life costs more if you’re disabled, whether you’re in work or not.
From Simon Antrobus, CEO at RNIB (the Royal National Institute of Blind People)

double quotation markPip is a lifeline for blind and partially sighted people who face the unavoidable extra costs of sight loss which can run into hundreds of pounds every month. The government’s ambition to end ‘dehumanising’ assessments could be transformative for people with sight loss who have faced the stress of pointless reassessments for permanent or degenerative eye conditions.
Timms explains two main goals from his review - short-term and long-term
For an alternative summary of what is in the report, here is the update published today by Stephen Timms and his two co-chairs, Dr Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan.
And here is an extract summarising the report.

double quotation markOur recommendations focus on two goals. 1. Improve Pip now Some people told us that the Pip process can feel dehumanising. We believe changes are needed now to reduce the negative impact it can have on those going through the current process. We believe the government should: -make the system simpler, more accessible, more personalised and less stressful -make assessments and decisions fairer, more consistent and higher quality -improve DWP systems and processes so they can support a reformed Pip 2. Fundamentally reform Pip We must move away from the current system that only focuses on what people cannot do. A reformed Pip should better reflect the barriers people face, the support they need and the extra costs they face. We believe a reformed Pip should: -be more straightforward to understand and manage -better recognise the extra costs and support needs that disabled people face -keep cash at the centre of Pip awards -give people the choice to access wider support and services in their communities - their choice should not affect their Pip entitlement
Here is a guide by Patrick Butler, the Guardian’s social affairs editor, to what the Timms report is proposing.
Farage rules out deal with Restore Britain unless it disavows antisemitic backers

Nigel Farage has said he might have a “civil chat” with Rupert Lowe but ruled out a deal with Restore Britain while some of its supporters promote antisemitism and think race should be linked to nationality, Rowena Mason reports.
Timms fails to assure Labour MPs that young Pip claimants won't lose out when under welfare bill coming next year

The Stephen Timms statement is now over. Relatively few Conservative MPs had questions for Timms, but many Labour MPs were in the chamber and leftwingers were out in force. Many of them were asking essentially the same question; while sympathetic to what Timms were proposing, they were expressed concern or alarm about Alan Milburn’s plan to scrap Pip for under-25s and they asked for an assurance that constituents getting Pip would not lose out under the legislation coming next year.

Timms was emollient and he repeatedly stressed his desire to ensure disabled people get the help they need. But he also defended the thrust of what Milburn is trying to achieve (see 3.12pm) and he refused to give cast-iron assurances. Final decisions about eligibility rules will come next year. (See 2.12pm.)

Jeremy Corbyn, the Your Party leader in parliament, said many Pip claimants were “terrified” of the future. He asked for an assurance that decisions about the future of Pip would be based on their needs, not on the demands of the Treasury.
Timms said Pip had to be sustainable.

And he said that, although his report was co-produced with disabled people, it also included a line saying coproduction would not be suitable for every stage of the process. Major decisions about spending had to be made the elected government, he said.
Timms says white paper on welfare reforms next year will include details of 'cost implications'
Mike Wood (Con) asked what assessment he had made of the impact his plans would have on welfare spending.
Timms said that the “cost implications” would be set out in the white paper next year.
Joshua Reynolds (Lib Dem) asked Timms for an assurance that disabled people who need support would not lose out as a result of the government legislation coming next year.
Timms said the intention was to ensure that people who incur extra costs because of a disability would continue to get Pip.

Iain Duncan Smith, who was the Tory work and pensions secretary who created Pip during the coalition government, said that Pip was established to replace the disability living allowance (DLA), which was seen to be “failing”. He accepted that the same process was happening again. He told Timms he supported what he was trying to do, and said there were “good elements” in the review.

Pip was intended to cut the amount of money being spent on disability benefits due to its strict eligibility requirements. But, in practice and over time, it failed to achieve the savings Duncan Smith had been expecting at the time.
Timms says Milburn made 'pretty compelling' case for getting rid of Pip for under-25s
Back in the Commons, Neil Duncan-Jordan, a Labour MP, asked Stephen Timms why Alan Milburn was proposing getting rid of Pip for people under the age of 25, when Timms was not recommending this.

Timms accepted that his report did not talk about age groups. But he said that Milburn had argued “pretty compellingly” that a “different approach” for young people was needed because they were at the start of their working lives.
Resolution Foundation thinktank says Timms and Milburn reports both failing to provide credible route to cutting welfare spending

The Resolution Foundation has issued its assessment of the Timms review. It says Timms is right to say that Pip needs fundamental reform, and it says there are “many similarities” between what Timms and Alan Milburn are saying.
But it also suggests that neither report is proposing a credible route to controlling welfare spending. This is from Lindsay Judge, research director at the RF.

double quotation markThe Timms Review has rightly concluded that the current system of Pip is not fit for purpose and makes sensible recommendations for overhauling it. Ensuring that payments better reflect the costs that disabled people face, and putting more emphasis on services, are both welcome and in line with the thinking set out in the Milburn review. Where the two reviews collide is in how to cut welfare spending. Milburn outlines implausibly large cuts on young people – equivalent to halving the total health and disability benefit support they receive – without saying how it would do this, while the Timms review avoids the question entirely. The government does need to contain the rising cost of disability benefits. The good news is that savings of over £4bn can be achieved while adopting much of the Timms review and making the system work better for all adults.
